newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh, India agree to share river water.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh, India agree to share river water.

text.p: Bangladesh and India on Sunday agreed to share the flow of a second common river, following up a a landmark treaty signed last year for sharing water from the mighty Ganges river.

"We have now agreed to share the water of the Teesta river. I am hopeful of solving all issues (between the two countries) through political will," Bangladesh Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak told a news conference after talks with his Indian counterpart, Sis Ram Ola.
The two countries share 54 common rivers, including the Ganges and Teesta.
Razzak said India had also expressed willingness to help Bangladesh to build a proposed dam to harness water from the Ganges.

"India has indicated its intention to consider (giving) technical assistance (to the proposed barrage," said a joint communique issued on Sunday following a two-day meeting of the India-Bangladesh Joint River Commission (JRC).
The Indian minister was due to fly back home later on Sunday after his three-day visit to Dhaka.
Officials said Bangladesh planned to build the Ganges barrage at Pangsha, 90 miles (150 km) west of Dhaka.
The 1,990-metre (2,170-yard) long dam, first planned in 1984, is designed to irrigate 1.35 million hectares of land and protect another 1.44 million hectares from floods.
The Ganges treaty in December 1996 was signed in New Delhi by Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who assumed power in June last year, and then Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
But it ran into trouble on the first year after Bangladesh reported low water flow into the country through India's Farakka barrage.
India built the barrage in 1954 to divert the flow of the Ganges, which irrigates much of northern India, before running down into Bangladesh.
Bangladesh complained to India that the flow dropped to nearly 10,000 cubic feet per second at one stage in March against a minimum of 35,000 stipulated in the treaty.
Razzak also admitted the water flow from the Ganges had been less, saying that a scientific committee was now studying the reasons that led to the shortfall of water level at Farakka point.
"We are unanimous about the full implementation of the Ganges treaty," he said.
Ola said there might be a "technical reason" behind the shortfall of water during the lean (dry) season.
"It (shortfall of water) will not happen (again). Whatever may be the treaty we will implement every part of it." he told the news conference.
He also said that India would adhere to any recommendations that the scientific committee would make to augment the Ganges flow.
